about: The words of the chain mission_north (Data/encounters/chain_mission_north_793.json; Design/content/chains/mission_north.md): carrying the mission north, Anskar to Birka in 829 and again about 852. Every title, intention, line and label key of its fourteen cards; an outcome text for every option and every branch of a chance (keys '...out_<option>', named in each option's note: the engine shows the effects' own facts, the outcome texts are for the integrator); five ending texts ('chain_mission_north.end.*'); the four news items the cards post; and one 'art.<card id>' line for each card's picture. People: Anskar, Witmar, King Bjorn, Herigar, Frideburg, the exile Anound, the hermit Ardgar, the priest Erimbert, King Horik and King Olaf are real and named; their words are invented, or are our own plain rendering of what Rimbert reports (Vita Anskarii c. 9-12, 17-20, 25-28; from memory of Robinson's translation of 1921, not quoted (?)). The old man at the thing and the man with the book on his fence are real and unnamed. The dealer, the chief, the man who throws the lots and the English captive are invented. A draft for the user to overwrite.

entries.text: Two monks and forty books

Two monks stand among the merchants who are making up a convoy for Birka. They have the emperor's gifts for the king of the Svear in sealed chests, and more books than most men here have seen in one place.
God keep you, shipmaster. I am Anskar, a monk of Corvey. They tell me you know this water, and that you do not charge a monk double. One of those may be true.
Men of the Svear came to the emperor and said their people would hear priests, and their king would allow it. So the emperor looked for someone to send. Nobody else stood up.
I am Witmar. I keep the books. Thirty-nine. Brother Anskar says nearly forty. He counts souls the same way.
The emperor's gifts and the book chests go in the big ship; she has the room. We two weigh little and eat less. It is Lent with us most of the year.
The merchants sail together when the wind serves. Will you take two of us aboard? We can pay a fare, and I am told I row badly but willingly.
Take the two monks aboard and sail in the convoy
Sail in the convoy, and let another hull carry them
Wish them a fair wind and go about your trade
Witmar counts the fare into your hand twice. Anskar comes aboard barefoot, sits where he is told and asks the name of every rope. The chests go into the big ship, and he watches them go.
A Dane with a broader hull takes the monks. You are one sail among the rest. Anskar lifts a hand to you across the water each morning, as if you had agreed to something.
He thanks you as though you had said yes. The convoy is still gathering. The book chests sit on the jetty under a hide with Witmar on top of them.
Sails out of the haze

Half-way, with land low to one side, the lookout counts sails coming out of the haze that are not the convoy's. They are long, low and under oars as well. The big ship with the monks' chests is the slowest hull among you.
Seven. No, nine. They have their masts down and they are rowing at us. Nobody rows at a stranger to ask the price of salt.
The merchants are shouting from hull to hull. They mean to close up round the big ship and fight. There are a good many of them, and they have done it before.
The books are in that ship. I ask nothing of you that you would not do for your own cargo. I only tell you where they are.
There is a beach under that low point, an hour off. And there is open water astern. Say which, while saying still counts for something.
Close up on the big ship and fight beside the merchants
Lay alongside her, take off one chest and run for the beach
Leave the convoy and run while they are busy with it

They come on twice. The first time the merchants beat them off, and the second time also, which nobody had looked for. By evening the long ships are hull down. The chests have not left the big ship. Witmar counts the books anyway.

The first attack is beaten off. The second is not. The merchants lose the ships and all that was in them and wade ashore with their lives. The emperor's gifts go north in a stranger's hull, and the books with them. Anskar says they will go on by land.

You touch the big ship long enough for two men to swing one chest across, and then you are away for the beach. Behind you the fight is lost. On the sand Witmar opens the chest: six books, a psalter on top. He says six is a number too.

A long ship is alongside her before you are. An oar is broken, a man is hurt, and what you had in the stern locker is gone with a boathook. You reach the beach with nothing of theirs. The monks walk up it after you, wet to the chest.

You put the helm over and the wind takes you clear. Nobody follows a small boat when a big one is to be had. That night the crew are quiet. Word comes later: the merchants lost everything, and the monks went on to Birka on foot.
The king asks his friends

The king of the Svear is on the island, and the prefect of the town has brought the two Frankish monks before him. The king has heard them. Now he looks along the bench at the merchants who came by the same road.
I am Herigar. I keep this town for the king. The Franks' king has sent ours a sword-belt, cups and a whole chest of calfskin. The king likes the belt. He is thinking about the calfskin.
I am Herigar. I keep this town for the king. Two envoys have walked in from the south with an emperor's greeting and no gifts. Such a man is a beggar or a brave one. The king wants to know which.
They say one small boat got clear of that convoy with her cargo whole. It is a good boat that knows when to leave. I say nothing against her master.
We lost what we were given to bring. We were not sent to bring cups. Tell him that, if he asks you. He will not believe it from me.
Six books, shipmaster. You have never seen Brother Witmar happy, so I tell you: that was it.
I am Bjorn. I have heard them. I will ask my friends what they think, and the men who trade in the south, who have seen this god at home. Then I will say whether these two may talk here.
You are of Dorstadt. Our men go there. Some come back with a new god and some with a cough. What do you say of it, in a few words? The king dislikes many.
Set a cask of your wine before the king, in the emperor's name
Say what you know: Dorestad trades under this god and does not starve
Leave kings and monks to each other and ask the price of cloth

The king has the cask broached where he sits. He drinks, and has Anskar drink from the same cup, and says an emperor who sends this may send his talkers too. Herigar tells you quietly that your ship will not be looked at hard this summer.

You say it in a few words. The king nods at the number of ships you name, not at the god. He gives the monks leave to stay and to speak, to those who want to hear. Herigar wants to hear, it turns out.
Herigar laughs and tells you: the good coloured cloth is short this year, and the women of the town know it. The king gives the monks leave without your help. He had mostly decided.
Calfskin with marks on it
A dealer has amber laid out on a square of pale skin with black marks in rows. Behind him, under a hide, lies a heap of the same: books with the boards torn off.
Good skin, scraped thin. It keeps the damp off amber. The marks do no harm. I had a man look, and he said they are not runes, so nobody is cursed.
They came with boards on, and some of the boards had bronze on them. The men who brought them kept the bronze. That is all I know of the men who brought them.
Eleven are whole inside. The rest got wet and stuck together like a bad cheese. I sell those by the leaf, for wrapping.
For the heap, silver to the weight of ninety pennies. You look at it as if it were worth more. If it is, you had better not say so until you have paid.
Buy the heap for 90 d, to carry back to the monks
Buy the heap for 90 d, and sell the best book in Francia
Tell him who would pay for them, and keep your silver

He weighs your silver and helps you carry the heap down in two hides. He throws in the leaf the amber sat on. Aboard, you find a name written small inside one of them, and a count in another hand: thirty-nine.

He weighs your silver and helps you carry the heap down. One gospel book is sound from end to end, and an abbot will pay a herd of calves for it. The rest you stow dry all the same. It seems wrong to wrap fish in it.

You tell him: a monk called Anskar, among the Danes or at Hammaburg, and he pays in silver for what the sea took. The dealer covers the heap again and moves it in from the door. He does not thank you, but he gives you a piece of amber for the walk back.
A church on Herigar's land
On the prefect's own ground behind the town stands a small new house of upright timbers with a cross cut over the door. Herigar is counting what it lacks. The Frankish monk is packing to go home.
I went into the water this spring and came out Herigar still, only wetter. This is my father's land. Nobody can tell me what I may build on it. Several have tried.
It lacks wine. The monks say their god will not be met in ale. Four casks of the Rhine sort, before the lake shuts next year. I pay over the market, since there is no market.
Two winters, shipmaster. I go home with a letter from the king, cut in his own marks by his own hand. Nobody at the emperor's court can read it. I can tell them what it says.
They tell me you have a heap of wet calfskin aboard that you paid too much for. Brother Witmar has not slept since he heard.
I was a boy on Lindisfarne when the ships came. I have tallied furs here for thirty winters. I can still say the psalms. I had forgotten that I could until that monk began one and stopped.
His master would let him go for the price of two thralls, since he is old and only reads. The monk has spent his silver on boys. He looked at me. I looked at you.
Take his order for Mass wine and nothing more
Lay the books without boards on the altar step
Give the monk passage south with the king's letter
Buy the Englishman free for 96 d and give him a place aboard
Herigar strikes your hand on it before witnesses: four casks, before the ice, at half as much again as wine fetches here. He says a church is like a ship. The hull is the cheap part.

Witmar goes through the heap on his knees and says the names of the books aloud like a man finding his children. Eleven whole. Anskar has Herigar weigh you two hundred pennies of silver and will not hear of less. Witmar teaches you the letters of your own name while he counts.

Anskar comes aboard with one sack and a flat stick wrapped in cloth. At sea he unwraps it and shows you the king's marks, and tells you what each one says, and you find you remember some. The fare is paid at parting, with a blessing you did not ask for.

His master takes the silver and the Englishman takes nothing with him but a stick he holds like a pen. Aboard he reads your tallies, finds two mistakes, both in your favour, and tells you so. He says his name is Tidwine. He has to think first.
No priest at Birka
The church behind the town is shut and its door is nailed. The prefect still wears his cross outside his cloak. An old woman in a good gown has sent to ask whether your ship carries wine.
They rose in a crowd. They killed the bishop's nephew Nithard in the house, bound the bishop and put him and his people out of the land. Then they went home and felt better for a week.
It was not the king's doing. Remember that. Here a crowd can do what a king cannot, and afterwards nobody did it.
I still speak at the thing. Last time it rained on all of them and not on me and my boy. They said it was the wind. It was a very narrow wind.
Your house brought the wine for the first Mass said on my land. I do not forget who came when it was easy. Now it is not easy.
I am Frideburg. I am old and there is no priest. I want a cask of wine to keep by me. When I am dying they are to put some in my mouth and commend me to God. I have told my daughter twice.

The bishop will not come back, and I do not blame him. But there is the other one, Anskar, among the Danes. Somebody must tell him there are Christians here who will die unshriven. I cannot leave the town.
Sell Frideburg a cask to keep for her last hour
Promise to carry Herigar's word to the archbishop
Say a trader has no part in a town's gods

She has the cask carried to her house and set on a shelf where she can see it from her chair. She pays without bargaining, which nobody in Birka has done before, and tells you she intends to keep you waiting for news of it.
Herigar gives you no letter, since nobody here can write one. He gives you a small silver cross from his own neck to show, and the words to say. You are to say them the same way each time.
Herigar says that is a trader's answer and he has given it himself, about other men's troubles. He sees to your berth as fairly as before. He does not ask you to eat.
The book on the fence

On the road up from the jetties a book hangs on a fence, tied with a cord, in the weather. People walk on the far side of the road. A grey man stands at his door across the yard and watches who stops.
My son brought it home when they broke up the bishop's house. Everyone took something. He took that. It had a clasp, and he thought his mother would like the clasp.
His mother is dead. He is dead. My daughter is dead. The cattle went after. I had a good farm two winters ago, and you can see what I have.
I asked a man who knows such things which god I had angered. He asked them all. Every one was content with me but one, and that one I had never met. He said something of that god's was under my roof.
So it hangs there. Anyone may have it. I have said so to everyone who passes. If you take it I will give you silver to carry it far. I do not sell it. Understand me. I do not sell it.
Untie it and carry it to the Christians of the town
Untie it and put it in your own chest to sell in Francia
Walk on the far side of the road like everyone else

The cord is stiff with rain. He puts cut silver in your hand before you have it loose and goes in and shuts his door. In Frideburg's house a man who can read a little reads it aloud to the rest, slowly, a psalm an evening. He shows you where the words begin.
He pays you to take it, and you take it further than he thinks. It is a psalter, hardly spoiled. The crew find out what is in the chest by the second day and steer as if the boat were made of eggs.
You go by on the far side. The grey man watches you all the way down the road. The book turns a little on its cord in the wind off the lake.
Thirty-two ships in the sound

Ships fill the sound: twenty-one of the Danes and eleven that belong to a king the Svear put out. The king who rules is far away. The townspeople have gone up to the fort on the rock, and the merchants are told what peace will cost.
King Anound was driven out of this land and has come to see it again. He has brought friends who were promised a rich town. He can ask them to leave it standing. They will want to know why.
A hundred pounds of silver. That is the why. The town has not got it. The merchants in harbour have, between them, and they are in harbour. You see how it stands.

Up at the fort they are killing beasts to every god they can name. I told them: you have vowed and given to those for years, and here are thirty-two ships. Vow to mine for once. They laughed. The Danes have not left, I notice.
Your share is small. You may pay it and be thanked. Or you may stand by me when I say it again to their faces, and be laughed at with me. I do not advise a third thing.
Weigh in your share with the merchants: 60 d
Stand by Herigar when he tells them to vow to Christ instead
Slip the mooring after dark and go out by the narrow sound

The silver goes out to the ships in sacks. The Danes say it is too little: any one merchant here has more. Then they throw lots, as they do, and their gods will not let them touch the place. Another lot sends them off against a town of the Slavs, a long way east. Herigar notes who paid.

They laugh at the two of you. Then, because nothing else has worked, the townsmen vow a fast and alms to Herigar's god. The Danes cast lots on whether to sack the town, and the lot says no. They cast again, and it sends them east against the Slavs. Nobody laughs at Herigar that week.

No moon, and the narrow sound is all rocks, but your men find it. By first light you are in open water with the hold whole. You hear later that the town paid, and the lots sent the Danes elsewhere. Nobody at Birka remarks on who was missing.

A guard boat lies across the narrow sound. They take what silver is to hand, crack a man's ribs with an oar and send you back to your berth. Herigar says nothing about it. He had advised against a third thing.
A hermit for Birka

By the new church at the harbour a greying bishop in a plain cloak is asking the shipmasters which of them goes to the lake of the Svear. Beside him stands a thin man with a sack, who looks at the ships as a man looks at a tooth-drawer.

Nearly seven years Birka has had no priest. There are Christians there who were baptised by my hand, and they are growing old. I cannot go myself this year. King Horik has only just let me have a roof here.
Herigar's cross reached me, and his words. You said them the way he told you to. I could hear him in it. It is why this man is standing here with his sack.

Some of the books the sea took came back. A dealer sent word that he had heard I pay. I bought my own psalter from him, and I think he had sold it to me once before. Nearly forty. Witmar always said thirty-nine.
You still have those books without boards? Then keep them dry as far as Birka. They were on their way there when they were stopped. It has only taken them twenty years.
I am Ardgar. I lived alone in a cell and was content. The bishop says God wants me in a town full of fur dealers. I have asked God about it and so far only the bishop has answered.
He needs a place in a ship, and a master who will see him ashore at Birka and into Herigar's hands. He eats almost nothing. He will tell you so himself, more than once.
Carry the hermit to Birka and take no fare
Carry him for the fare
Tell him your hull is full this voyage

The bishop does not press the fare on you twice. He marks you down somewhere behind his eyes instead. Ardgar comes aboard, finds the least comfortable place in the boat by himself and seems easier there.
The bishop counts out the fare in the new pennies of this place. Ardgar comes aboard, finds the least comfortable place in the boat by himself and seems easier there.
The bishop thanks you and turns to the next master along the jetty. A Dane takes the hermit two days later. You hear he was seasick as far as the islands and prayed the rest of the way.
The archbishop wants a ship
The archbishop is going to Birka himself, twenty days by sea, at past fifty. With him are a young priest and a man of King Horik's who carries the king's token in a bag round his neck.
Herigar is dead. He had the sacrament from Ardgar's hand at the last, and Frideburg after him, and then Ardgar came home to his cell. So Birka has no priest again and no Herigar. I am going myself.
He died with a priest beside him because a ship carried one there. I have not forgotten whose ship.
King Horik sends his own man with me, and his token, to King Olaf. He bids the man say he has never in his life seen so good a man as I am. I told him kings should be careful what they swear to.
I am Erimbert. Bishop Gautbert is my uncle. He was bound and put out of Birka, and my cousin Nithard was killed there. My uncle says it is not fitting that he go back. So he has sent me.
The last time I went I trusted to a convoy and a great many merchants. This time I would rather have one master who knows where the beaches are.
Twenty days, if the wind is kind. Three of us and what a church needs. Will you take us? I row no better than I did.
Take the archbishop, the priest and the king's man aboard
Take them, and buy a small bell for Birka at your own cost
Sail in company and carry only their stores
Say you are not bound that way yet

The king's man sits in the bow with his hand on the bag at his neck. The young priest is sick over the lee side with great patience. The archbishop asks the name of every rope, and this time remembers them.

A founder in the town has a hand bell of bronze he made for a Frisian who never came back for it. You pay him and wrap it in sheepskin so it will not speak at sea. The archbishop looks at the bundle and then at you, and says the heathen think such a thing unlawful. He does not say leave it.
They take passage in a bigger hull, and you carry their meal, their wax and their altar cloths, and keep her in sight. The archbishop lifts a hand to you across the water each morning.
He says he will be here some days yet, since King Horik's man is still taking leave of his wife. The young priest looks relieved at any delay at all.
A new god, or King Eric

Birka is talking of one thing. A man has stood up and said he sat at the gods' own meeting, and brings their word. The archbishop's friends tell him to buy his life and go. He has asked the king to eat with him instead.
You have heard what the man said. He was at the meeting of the gods who own this land. They say: we gave you peace and good years for a long time, and now you grudge us our due.
And they say: if you must have more gods, and we are not enough, we will take Eric who was your king into our number. He can be your new god. At least he knows the way here.
My friends here tell me to give the king all I brought, as the price of leaving alive. I have given it to him as a gift at his meat instead. It is the same silver. It reads differently.
I am Olaf. I liked your meal and I like your Danish king's word of you. But priests were here before, and the people drove them out. Not the king. The people.
So I will ask the gods by lot whether they allow it. Then I will ask the people at the thing. That is our custom. Here such things rest with the whole people and not with the king.
You are of Dorstadt, and the people will look at you when it comes to talking. They trust a man who sells them cloth above a man who sells them heaven. Which way will you talk?
Tell the king's men what the cross is worth on the Dorestad road
Drink with the men who want King Eric among the gods
Ask the king what a stranger may keep on his own plot

You tell them plainly: at Dorestad a baptised Svea eats with the merchants and a heathen one eats with his crew, and prices are made where the merchants eat. They follow that better than the archbishop's sermon. He does not seem to mind.

They are good company and they pour well. King Eric was a fair judge of a horse, they say, and will make a sensible god. Before the night is out one of them has offered you marten skins at a price for friends. The archbishop sees who you sat with.

The king thinks about it. A man's plot is his own, he says, inside his fence, so long as he pays his due for it. Herigar built on his, and nobody could stop him. Whether a stranger may have such a plot is for the thing. He looks at you with more interest than before.
The lot in the open field

The king and his chiefs have gone out to the open field, as the custom is. An old man shakes cut slips of wood in his two hands over a white cloth. The question has been said aloud: do the gods allow the Christians' worship here.
Stand back from the cloth. All of you. The gods can see over your heads, but I cannot.
Whatever falls, falls. I will carry it to the people as it lies, and I will not be asked to throw twice because some man dislikes it.
I have fasted three days over this. Now it comes down to how an old man opens his hands. I do not complain. The apostles drew lots for the twelfth of their number.
I have thrown for kings and for a man who had lost a pig. The slips do not know the difference. People always ask me whether they do.
Stand among the merchants and watch it fall
Vow alms for the poor of Dorestad, aloud, whichever way it falls
Send the thrower 80 d beforehand, to see the slips fall kindly
Send him 80 d to let it fall against the stranger god

The slips lie on the cloth. The old man bends, looks a long while, and stands up with his hand on his back. The gods allow it, he says. The king lets out his breath. The matter goes to the thing in two days.

The slips lie on the cloth. The old man bends, looks a long while, and stands up with his hand on his back. The gods do not allow it, he says. Nobody speaks. The archbishop bows to the king as if he had been handed a cup.

You say it aloud, with the amount, and the merchants turn to look. The thrower says the gods of this field take no interest in the poor of Dorestad, but that it was handsomely said. Your crew stand a little straighter. Then he opens his hands.

The old man took your silver the night before without a word and throws today without a glance at you. The gods allow it, he says. You will never know what you bought. He is the only man in the field who looks entirely at ease.

The old man took your silver the night before. Today he lays it on the white cloth beside the slips, in front of the king, and says a stranger tried to help the gods make up their minds. Then he throws. The gods do not allow it. The king does not look at you at all.

The old man took your silver the night before without a word. The gods do not allow it, he says. Your friends of the other evening are careful not to smile. The archbishop bows to the king as if he had been handed a cup.
The old man took your silver the night before without a word. The gods allow it, he says, and looks straight at you while he says it. He keeps the silver. There is nobody you can complain to.
The old man at the thing

The king's crier has said it before the whole people: the lot allows the Christians' worship, and the king asks what they will have. The shouting goes on a long time. Then an old man gets up, and they let him speak because of his years.
Hear me, king and people. Many of us know this god. He helps those who hope in him. More than one man here has called on him in danger at sea, and is here to be shouted at.
Some of us went to Dorstadt and took up this worship there of our own will, because we saw it was of use. We sailed a long way to get it.

Now the way there is beset with pirates, and a man may lose his ship going. Why then do we refuse at our own door what we went so far to find? If our own gods are slow, it is good to have this one's favour as well.
You have heard the lot and you have heard him. Is there a man here who has been where he speaks of, and will say whether it is so?
The thrower wears a new arm-ring today. I do not ask where a poor old man finds silver. I only say I would rather have lost honestly, and I think you know it.
Stand up after him: you are of Dorestad, and it is as he says
Lay the book and the bell before them, and say what your house has carried
Ask the thing for the church on your own plot, as Herigar had his
Stand up and count out what the last priests cost this town

You say it in few words: there are churches at Dorestad and ships at Dorestad, and the one has not sunk the other. The people shout their yes. The king gives a hall of his own to be the church, and the archbishop buys a plot beside it for the priest. Its storehouse has room for your goods.

You lay the book on the ground before them, and the bell on the book. You say where each has been, and who was carried, and who stood where. Then you ring it once. The heathen hold a bell unlawful. Nobody moves to stop it. The king says he will hear that sound again, and the people shout their yes.

You ask for no new law. A plot inside a fence, held of the king for the common due, and a priest kept on it at your cost, for any trader who wants him. The thing likes it: no hall of the king's, no bishop's man answering to no one. The traders who go south pay in furs for their share. The archbishop thanks you carefully.

You count it out for them on your fingers: a bishop's nephew dead in the house, a farm emptied over one book, a hundred pounds of silver to thirty-two ships. The old man calls you a seller of both sides. The people shout their no. Your friends bring furs to the jetty after dark. The archbishop goes home in another ship.
The gods say no

The slips fell against it, in front of every chief. The king has sent the archbishop a ring and a courteous word, and the word is no. An old man of the town has come down to the jetty and is angry with all of you.
I cannot carry to the people a thing the gods have refused. I told him so before I threw. He is a good man, and my brother the Danish king was right about him. He must go home.
And tell the Frisian that at this market we weigh silver in the open, on a scale, where both sides can see the pans.
I was robbed coming here the first time and came on. This time nobody has robbed me. I have only been told no, politely. I find that I do not know what to do with it.
Slips of wood! I have called on that god in a gale off the Danish islands and I am standing here. I would have said so at the thing, if there were to be a thing.
Herigar asked no lot. He built on his own land and let them talk. The gods were asked about the whole town. Nobody has asked them about one man's fence.
Carry the archbishop home, and say nothing clever on the way
Ask the king to throw once more, on a smaller question: a stranger's own plot
Bring the old man before the chiefs, lot or no lot
Take the thanks of the men who wanted it so

Twenty days back. He is silent for the first three, and then asks the names of the ropes again, to be sure. At Sliesthorp he weighs you the silver that was meant for a priest's house, since no priest will need it, and says that whoever touches you or your goods in his see touches him.

The king does not throw twice on one question. This is another question, he says, and a small one, and has the old man shake the slips again. A stranger may keep his own god inside his own fence. The traders who go south pay in furs for their share of it. The archbishop sails home with half of what he came for, and it is in your name.

The king hears you out and says he told everyone beforehand that he would not be asked to throw twice. He is not angry. He is finished. The archbishop goes home, and on parting weighs you the silver meant for a priest's house and takes you under his hand, because you tried.

The old man does not ask leave. He walks in among the chiefs and tells them about the gale, and the islands, and who he called on. Then he asks which of them wants to tell the seamen of Birka that they may not thank the god who brought them home. The king puts it to the thing after all. The people shout their yes.

The chiefs hear the old man with respect and do not change their minds. The gods were asked, and answered. The king is short with you for pressing it. The archbishop goes home, and on parting weighs you the silver meant for a priest's house and takes you under his hand, because you tried.

They come down to the jetty after dark with sable, which they do not sell to strangers, and the word that a plot by the stone jetties is yours when you want it. The archbishop sails in another hull. He does not look across.

This year the Svear asked their gods and their people, and both said that the priests might stay. Erimbert kept the church at Birka. The archbishop went home in the same ship. After his death no priest came for seventy years.

This year the Svear asked their gods and their people, and both said that the priests might stay. A bell was rung at Birka before the whole thing, and the king had it hung. When the archbishop died the church on the island did not shut, for the traders had come to tell the hours by it.

This year the Svear would have no bishop's church, but let a Frisian keep a priest on his own plot at Birka for any trader who wanted one. The archbishop called it half a loaf. It was still there when he was dead, since it belonged to a house and not to a see.

This year the Svear sent the archbishop home and took their dead king Eric among their gods. No priest came to Birka again in that age. A Frisian house had a plot by the stone jetties there, and bishops on the Rhine knew its name.

This year the lot fell against the Christians at Birka, and the archbishop went home in a Frisian's boat. The Svear took their dead king Eric among their gods. The archbishop did not send again, but he kept his hand over the house that carried him.
At Birka the lot and the thing have both allowed the Christians' worship. The king of the Svear has given a hall for a church, and a Frankish priest stays there.
A bell has been rung before the thing at Birka and the king of the Svear has had it hung in the new church. Men who go to Dorstadt say the lake is a Christian's road now.
The Svear would have no bishop's church at Birka, but a Frisian keeps a priest on his own plot there, and any trader may hear Mass inside his fence.
The Svear have sent the archbishop home from Birka. They say their dead king Eric sits among the gods now, and that they had gods enough.

A spring morning at a timber jetty, hulls being loaded for the north. Two young tonsured monks in black habits: one thin and barefoot, talking to a shipmaster; the other sitting on a stack of iron-bound chests under a hide, counting on his fingers.

Open sea in thin haze, a low shore to one side. A huddle of merchant ships round one big slow hull; out of the haze long low ships under oars with their masts lowered. In the near boat a monk stands, looking at the big ship.

A dim hall on Birka by firelight. A king on the high seat with a cup; before him two travel-worn monks with mud to the knee; a broad man with keys and a staff standing between them and a bench of merchants. All eyes on one Frisian on the bench.

A beach market under a grey sky. A dealer squats behind a square of written parchment spread with lumps of amber; behind him a hide half pulled back from a heap of books with their boards torn away, the leaves cockled by water.

Summer on Birka, behind the town. A small new church of upright split timbers with a cross cut over the door; a heavy man counting on his fingers at the doorway; a monk tying a sack; an old thrall in a rope collar holding a stick like a pen.

The same small church years on, weathered, its door nailed shut with a plank. A grey-bearded man with a silver cross worn openly stands before it in the rain, dry. At a house door behind, an upright old woman in oval brooches and beads.

A muddy road up from the jetties on a wet, windy day. A book with a clasp hangs by a cord from a wattle fence; passers-by keep to the far side; across an empty yard a grey man watches from the door of a house with no smoke.

Evening over the sound at Birka: the water crowded with thirty ships, shields along their sides. On the stone jetty a line of merchants weighing sacks of silver on folding scales; above the town, the fort on its rock, with fires and people on the rampart.

The harbour at Sliesthorp on a bright day, a new plank church by the water. A greying bishop in a plain cloak speaks to shipmasters on the jetty; beside him a gaunt hermit with one sack eyes the boats with dread.

A small boat being stowed at Sliesthorp in early summer. The old archbishop steps aboard with a hand from a sailor; a pale young priest waits behind; a Danish king's man with a bag at his neck; in the hold, a bell wrapped in sheepskin.

A feast in a hall on Birka at night. The archbishop serves the king of the Svear at his own table, gifts laid out between the dishes; down the benches chiefs lean together and mutter; one of them is looking at a Frisian merchant, a horn held out.

An open field outside the town under a high pale sky. A ring of chiefs and a king stand back from a white cloth on the grass; an old man holds cut slips of wood in his cupped hands above it; the archbishop apart, head bowed.

The thing at Birka at midday: a great crowd on a slope, the king on a stone, a crier beside him. One very old man is on his feet with an arm raised, speaking; the crowd has gone quiet. At the edge, the archbishop and a Frisian merchant.

The stone jetty at Birka on a grey morning. The archbishop sits on a sea chest with a gold ring in his open hand, looking at it; a king's man walks away up the jetty; an old townsman shakes his stick at a moored Frisian boat.
